content: The Trendelenburg position involves placing the patient flat on their back (supine position) with their feet elevated higher than their head. This is in contrast to the reverse Trendelenburg position, where the body is tilted in the opposite direction. The Trendelenburg position is commonly used in abdominal and gynecological surgeries as it provides better access to the pelvic organs by allowing gravity to pull the intestines toward the head. The position is named after Friedrich Trendelenburg, a German surgeon. Historically, hypotensive patients (those with low blood pressure) were placed in the Trendelenburg position to increase cerebral perfusion pressure (blood flow to the brain). However, a 2008 review highlighted adverse effects associated with this practice and recommended avoiding it. Instead, the passive leg-raising test is now considered a more effective clinical tool for guiding fluid resuscitation. The Trendelenburg position was once the standard first-aid position for shock and was also used for injured scuba divers. While some experienced divers still believe it is appropriate, modern scuba first-aid guidelines no longer recommend elevating the feet above the head. This is because the position can exacerbate regurgitation, airway problems, brain swelling, and breathing difficulties, and it has not been proven to provide any benefit. For victims of submersion injuries, the general rule is supine is fine, unless there is fluid in the airway or the patient is breathing, in which case they should be positioned on their side. Due to its effects on breathing and airway complications, the Trendelenburg position has been used in waterboarding. In obstetrics, the Trendelenburg position may be employed in specific situations, such as when a woman’s cervix is too swollen to fully dilate to 10 centimeters, during a prolapsed umbilical cord to relieve pressure on the cord and improve oxygen delivery to the fetus, or to assist in rotating a posterior fetus during pregnancy or delivery. The position is also beneficial in reducing an abdominal hernia. In vascular access procedures, the Trendelenburg position is used when placing a central venous line. Gravity assists in filling and distending the upper central veins, such as the internal jugular or subclavian veins, making it easier to insert the line. It is also used for placing an external jugular peripheral line for the same reason. However, it is not utilized for the placement of femoral central venous lines.
